analysis.one_liner: Bans new oil, gas, and coal leasing on federal land and offshore waters.
analysis.headline: The bill got no hearing, no vote, and no floor action after being referred to the Senate Energy Committee in April 2021, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended all new federal leases for coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, and gas, both on public land and in offshore waters including the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic oceans [S2] [S3]. It would also have canceled existing leases in three Alaska offshore areas within 60 days [S2] [S3]. Narrow exceptions were allowed for imminent national security threats and to avoid breaching existing lease contracts [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received any further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, in the form of avoided climate damage and cleaner air: the bill's own findings state that ending new federal leases would prevent about 90 percent of the potential emissions from federal fossil fuels [S3]. Communities near leases, drilling sites, and coal operations — including coastal communities facing offshore drilling — would benefit from reduced pollution and spill risk [S2] [S3]. Publicly owned land and waters would be managed for climate goals rather than resource extraction [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and the climate-exposed public

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management from issuing, renewing, reinstating, or extending any nonproducing lease or any exploration or production authorization in the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic oceans, and any other outer Continental Shelf area [S2] [S3].

Bars the Bureau of Land Management from any new lease sale, new lease, or renewal, reinstatement, or extension of nonproducing leases for onshore coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, and gas under the Mineral Leasing Act [S2] [S3].
Requires cancellation within 60 days of existing leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea in the Alaska outer Continental Shelf [S2] [S3].
Includes exceptions only for imminent national security threats and where enforcing the ban would likely cause a court to find a material breach of a pre-existing lease contract [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers lose access to new federal minerals and, in the Alaska offshore areas specified, existing leases [S2] [S3]. The federal government and states that share royalty revenue from federal leasing would forgo that income, and the bill's critics would point to the risk of reduced domestic supply, shifting production to private or state land with different rules, and compensation claims from existing leaseholders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal producers; royalty-receiving states

drawbacks.text: Federal energy royalties are shared with states and the Treasury, so ending new leases means giving up that revenue stream, and reduced federal supply could put upward pressure on energy prices in the near term, an honest cost supporters would have to acknowledge.

Production does not disappear when federal leasing stops: it can shift to private or state land outside federal control, meaning emissions and drilling may continue with weaker public oversight, partially undercutting the climate goal.

Canceling existing Alaska leases would invite lawsuits and compensation claims from leaseholders, which is exactly why the bill built in a breach-of-contract exception — an acknowledgment that parts of the ban are legally fragile [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The climate and pollution benefits are large but long-term and diffuse, while the costs — lost royalties, possible price pressure, and legal exposure — are concentrated on producers and leaseholding states. The bill's own findings say ending new federal leases would prevent about 90 percent of potential federal-fossil-fuel emissions [S3]. The honest weakness is leakage: banning federal leases does not ban drilling, so some production and emissions would move to non-federal land. On the merits it was a serious, if sweeping, attempt to use federal control of land and waters as a climate lever, not a measure designed to shield a special interest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on April 14, 2021 with six original cosponsors: Sens. Sanders, Leahy, Menendez, Warren, Van Hollen, and Padilla [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — ever followed [S5].
In total the bill drew 8 cosponsors: 1 of the Senate's 2 independents and 7 of its 48 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal producers keep their access to new federal leases on public land and offshore waters, since the ban never advanced. States and companies that rely on federal royalty and leasing income are spared the disruption the bill would have caused.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor; it was referred to the Energy Committee the same day and never advanced [S1] [S5].

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Joe Manchin, D-WV, in the 117th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no committee action after the April 14, 2021 referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 8 cosponsors were Democrats or independents — 7 of 48 Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee without any vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists [S4].

industries.note: The bill ends their access to new federal offshore and onshore leases and cancels existing leases in three Alaska offshore areas [S2] [S3]. Their interest in continued access to federal minerals runs directly against the climate and air-quality benefit to the public.

New coal leases on federal land under the Mineral Leasing Act are expressly barred [S3]. Continued access to cheap federal coal comes at the cost of the mining and combustion pollution borne by nearby communities.

industries.industry: Oilfield services and offshore drilling contractors
industries.note: With no new leases or exploration authorizations in the Gulf, Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic waters, the pipeline of future offshore contracts shrinks [S2] [S3].
The bill declares a policy of promoting 'a rapid transition to a clean energy economy' by keeping federal fossil fuels in the ground, which shifts federal land and waters toward alternatives [S3].
